Artificial pancreas for 4 year old boy in Australia

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Break through technology in the treatment of Type 1 Diabetes

Summary:
Xavier Hames like many Type 1 Diabetes sufferers was diagnosed as a toddler; it is most prevalent in small children and young adults. His mother tells the story about trying to prick the finger of her small child 4/5 times a day to check his sugar levels and then having to give him regular injections. She talks about the fear of putting him to bed, the fear that her child will have a hypoglycemic attack at night and go into a coma.

Dr. Jones/Official spokesperson for the new technology, explains what Type 1 diabetes is and what treatments have been available up until today. He introduces us to the insulin pump, which has been around since 2003. It required human intervention to monitor and release the insulin.

Fast forward to 2015 and the old insulin pump has taken on a new form, this new pump can actually predict when glucose levels have become dangerously low and therefore stop the release of insulin. The pump is starting to behave like an artificially pancreas, allowing both mother and child a solid nights sleep. This ‘artificial pancreas’ also allows Xavier to live more like a normal 4-year-old boy, he can have a bowl of pasta or eat the food at a party.

To bring it home we speak to pediatric diabetic specialists dr. Segal about this new technology, when it will make it to South Africa, if it will be affordable and whether or not this is a practical solution for Type 1 diabetes sufferers over here.

Dr. Jones/Spokesperson explains how long this pump has been in development and what is next for type 1 diabetes patients. Xavier is the first patient, but when will this be available world and what does it cost.




Expert:
Dr. David Segal
Dr. Princess Margaret Hospital
Ms. Naomi Hames
Mr. Xavier Hames

Press Release:


Almost an artificial pancreas
When he was only 22 months old, four-year old Xavier Hames was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. His parents spent each day of the next two years weighing everything he ate and then injecting him with the right amount of insulin. Carte Blanche meets the 4-year-old who has now become the first recipient of a ground-breaking insulin pump that has taken the world one step closer to an artificial pancreas.


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
00:00 Xavier Hames and his family in their home Intro music

V/O: Xavier Hames is a four year old boy from Perth Australia. He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when he was 22 months old. In January this year he was the first the first patient in the world to receive a breakthrough medical advancement in the treatment of diabetes.
00:21 Naomi Hames He had all the classic symptoms. Looking back it was clear as day but you don’t think that at 22 months he’s going to get diagnosed with diabetes.
When Xavier was first diagnosed he went into what’s known as ketoacidosis, so he had very high ketones and that’s where he started getting very very sick, urinating, drinking, passing out.
00:50 Xavier and his sister Lilly playing in the house Naomi: Xavier, Lilly go and sit down now.
Xavier: No
Naomi: Well then no yoghurt, that’s ok.
00:56 Dr. David Segal Type 1 diabetes is a type of diabetes that children get more than adults that’s usually because the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin are damaged or destroyed by your immune system.
01:06 Prof. Tim Jones So your body normally will protect the glucose cells and keep it above a certain level to keep the body working and to keep the brain working. So if it goes low the brain stops working you can end up having seizures and unconsciousness and rarely even death.
01:23 Dr. David Type 1 diabetes gets managed by multiple daily injections or insulin pump therapies. So you have either have to do lots of injections each at every meal time plus background insulins or you can use an insulin pump to deliver insulin continuously in the background or and at meal times across the day. Because the balance with blood sugar control is to prevent lots of highs which are damaging for the brain and prevent lots of lows which is also damaging to the young brain. So now you are trying to keep blood sugars in a very narrow target range and the risk is to be still a little bit too high or still a little bit too low.
01:55 Naomi Previously when we were on injections we’d either have to take his injections with us and I tell you, injecting a child you get some funny looks. Because people all they’d see is a needle and injection and you’ve got to think of Xavier as well, you can’t just go randomly and be injecting into his little body it’s his body.
02:17 Xavier and his family interacting Music

Naomi: Eat your peas and corn and you can have that yoghurt.
Xavier: I love you
Naomi: I love you too
02:24 Xavier and his family interacting V/O: Food is instrumental in the treatment of type 1 diabetes. Everything Xavier eats had to be weighed and the amount of insulin he’s then given is measured according to how many carbohydrates he’s going to eat.
02:39 Prof. Tim I look at diabetes as a huge burden for people and families. You have to test regularly, you have to think about everything you do, exercise, eat, even emotions can change. It’s relentless, it’s every minute of the day and also night. Many of the families I look after one of the parents doesn’t sleep through the night.
The burden and the psychological distress to people with type one diabetes is very high. So that’s one of the motivations to try and get automated systems to make life easier for people
03:15 Naomi: Xavier can you come and get tested please.
03:18 V/O: Earlier this year Xavier Hames was given a ground breaking insulin pump by Dr. Tim Jones, who headed up the trial on this medical innovation.
03:28 Prof. Tim Pumps have been around since to 80s but obviously the technology has improved dramatically in the last 20years so the pump I’ve given to Xavier was the next step, the most recent step in the pathway towards a full on efficient pancreas. So this pump if you wear a sensor with it, has a formula in there and alga rhythm built within the pump that monitors the glucose levels and if it predicts that the glucose levels are going to drop dangerously low in the next 20 to 30 minutes it will switch off the insulin. So it’s a safety device and it’s a big step forward because low blood glucose is really important on how we manage diabetes.
04:18 Xavier and his family interacting V/O: Xavier’s pump has to be changed every 2 – 3 days. The insulin from the pump has to be released through a tiny catheter which goes into the fatty tissue using a small needle, the pump itself is then placed in a pouch which Xavier ears around his waist.
04:35 Steve and Naomi You know it’s not just intake of food and then you know put the insulin in front of him, you also have to take into account the exercises he’s having that day, like swimming, we go swimming every Monday, uhmmmm and we’ve got things on the pump that we can set in there like ok, this is swimming day, so for this amount of time you are getting less insulin, which is fantastic.
04:57 Xavier and his family interacting Naomi: You want to do some painting in your new book?
Xavier: Yes
05:00 Xavier and his family interacting People with type 1 diabetes have to be constantly monitored. But with this new pump, Xavier’s parents can finally get to sleep at night, as it will prevent him from having a hypoglycaemic attack or alert them if his glucose is too low. This pump can also be used by adults
05:20 Xavier and his family interacting Xavier: Why does it go up this way?
Naomi: Because that’s how much your little cannula is. Go to daddy and ask for your pump belt
05:32 Dr. David It’s mostly on the low end that we get concerned that people tend to run their blood sugars higher to stay away from the lows because the highs you don’t feel bad with but the lows you feel terrible with and they are more dangerous as a once of event. So most people overweigh the lows. Now, with this technology it’s going to allow you to get closer to the target zone without getting too many lows. The previous pump that’s out that currently does send blood sugars and suspends if you really gone low is more like having an airbag in your car rather than using your break. So having a sensor that can, sense and reduce the insulin that’s going in is a major advancement and peace of mind for parents.
06:09 Xavier walking with his pump Music
06:15 Prof. Tim In the last 10 years we’ve put a lot of effort into working on technology as a way of improving treatments, reducing risks of low glucose and improving the burden of diabetes. And this so far has shown a lot of promise with the technological developments that have occurred. This new pump was one step along the way it’s not an artificial pancreas at all but it’s a step and it shows that technology can work and can improve lives.
06:47 Xavier eating and laughing Music
06:52 Dr. David Closed loop pumps which is full artificial pancreas are probably 2 to 3 years away from having a viable commercial product on the market. The pump that Xavier has is not currently available in South Africa but we are hoping towards the latter half of this year it will be available.
07:05 Naomi He’s like perfect. But then there’s something that can’t work and you can’t control that. And that sucks. And I don’t think about it very much, very hard because it can be very overwhelming.
07:20 Naomi and Steven putting Xavier to sleep Music
07:25 Steven and Naomi Diabetes used to be a death thing, you survived a little while then you died, that was it and……

Now you can live normally. You can go to birthday parties, you can go swimming, all that sort of stuff. You just have to do a few extra things in life.
07:46 Naomi putting Xavier to bed Naomi: I love you
Xavier: I love you
Naomi: Very much
Xavier: Very Much
Singing together: Have sweet dreams baby boy.
Naomi: Goodnight.
08:00 END
